2016  NBQB
185
COURT
FILE NO:  FDF-237-16

IN THE COURT OF QUEEN’S BENCH OF NEW BRUNSWICK

FAMILY
DIVISION

JUDICIAL DISTRICT OF FREDERICTON

IN
THE MATTER OF AN APPLICATION

FOR
THE RETURN OF CHILDREN under

Article
12 of the Hague Convention on

the
Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction

BETWEEN:

The Attorney General as Central
Authority for the Province of New Brunswick for

I.R.,

Applicant,

and

R.P.,

Respondent

REASONS FOR DECISION

Date of Hearing:                    September
19, 2016

Date of Decision:                   October
17, 2016

Before:                                               Madam
Justice Anne D. Wooder

Representation of Parties at Hearing:

Karen LeBlanc, Esqe., Solicitor for the
Attorney General as Central Authority for the Province of New Brunswick

Joseph FitzPatrick, Esq., Solicitor
for the Respondent

I.
INTRODUCTION
:

[
1
.]                  The Attorney
General, as the Central Authority for the Province of New Brunswick, has filed
this application for I.R. seeking the return to Israel of the three R.'s
children pursuant to  the
Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of
International Child Abduction
, Can. T.S. 1983 No. 35 (hereinafter “the
Hague
Convention
” or “the
Convention
”).   R.P. opposes the application.

[
2
.]                  The
Hague Convention
,
a multilateral treaty, was signed by Canada in October   1980.   Effect was
given to the
Convention
by way of provincial legislation. In New  Brunswick,
the
International Child Abduction Act
, R.S.N.B. 2011, c. 175 is the
current  version of the  statute that gives force to the
Convention
.

II.

ISSUE
:

[
3
.]                  The sole
issue is whether the three children must be returned to the State of Israel           pursuant
to the
Convention
.

III.
THE
PROCEEDING
:

[
4
.]                  The first
Requisition as required by Article 16 of the
Convention
was filed on May
17, 2016. The subsequent application was dismissed without prejudice by a
justice of this court on June 9, 2016.  The second Requisition was filed on June
9, 2016.  Almost three months later, on September 1, 2016, this second application
was filed.

[
5
.]                  Both Mr. I.R.
and Ms. R.P. attended for the hearing.  Neither one of        them testified.  Ms.
R.P. did file a Responding Document and an affidavit.  Mr. I.R. filed no
affidavit in support of this application.  Included in the material filed by
the Attorney General, at page 100 of the Record on Application, is a copy of an
affidavit filed by Mr. I.R. in support of a Preliminary Notice of Motion (the
“Motion”) that he had previously filed under
New Brunswick’s
Family Services
Act

S.N.B. 1980, c. F-2.2.

IV.
THE
CONVENTION
:

[
6
.]                  The objects
of the
Convention
are set out in Article 1 as follows:

(a)

To
secure the prompt return of children wrongfully             removed to or
retained in any Contracting State; and,

(b)

To
ensure that rights of custody and access under the law of         one
Contracting State are effectively respected in the other      Contracting
States.

[
7
.]                  Israel became a Contracting
State to the
Convention
on December 1, 1991

[
8
.]                  Article
3 of the
Convention
provides that:

The removal or the retention of a child is
to be considered wrongful where

(a)

it is in breach of
rights of custody attributed to a person, an  institution or any other body,
either jointly or alone, under the             law of the State in which the
child was habitually resident           immediately before the removal or
retention; and

(b)

at the time of removal
or retention those rights were actually            exercised, either jointly or
alone, or would have been so           exercised but for the removal or
retention.

The rights of custody mentioned in sub-paragraph
a)

above, may arise in particular by operation of law or by reason of a
judicial or administrative decision, or by reason of an agreement having legal
effect under the law of that State.

[
9
.]                 Article
4 provides that the
Convention
applies only to children under the age of
16 years who were habitually resident in a Contracting State immediately before
a    breach of custody or access rights.

[
10
.]                While the
Convention’
s
objects include the protection of rights of access, Article            8
provides for a return application
only
in cases where custody rights
have been  breached.

[
11
.]                Article 12
provides for the mandatory return “forthwith” of a child.

Article 12

Where the child has
been wrongfully removed or retained in terms of Article 3, and, at the date of
the commencement of the proceedings before the judicial or administrative
authority of the Contracting State where the child is, a period of less than
one year has elapsed from the date of the wrongful removal or retention, the
authority concerned shall order the return of the child forthwith.

The judicial or
administrative authority, even where the proceedings have been commenced after
the expiration of the period of one year referred to in the preceding
paragraph, shall also order the return of the child, unless it is demonstrated
that the child is now settled in its new environment.

Where the judicial or
administrative authority in the requested State has reason to believe that the
child has been taken to another State, it may stay the proceedings or dismiss
the application for the return of the child.

[
12
.]                There are four
circumstances in which a court is not bound by Article 12 even     though the
elements of Article 3 have been established.  Three are set out in Article 13,            which
reads as follows:

Article 13

Notwithstanding the
provisions of the preceding Article, the judicial or administrative authority
of the requested State is not bound to order the return of the child if the
person, institution or other body which opposes its return establishes that:

(a)       the person,
institution or other body having the care of the person   of the child was not
actually exercising the custody rights at the  time of removal or retention, or
had consented to or subsequently             acquiesced in the removal or
retention: or

(b)       there is a
grave risk that his or her return would expose the child      to physical or
psychological harm or otherwise place the child in   an intolerable situation.

The judicial or
administrative authority may also refuse to order the return of the child if it
finds that the child objects to being returned and has attained an age and
degree of maturity at which it is appropriate to take account of its views.

In considering the
circumstances referred to in this Article, the judicial and administrative
authorities shall take into account the information relating to the social
background of the child provided by the Central Authority or other competent
authority of the child’s habitual residence.

The fourth is set out
in Article 20 which provides that:

Article 20

The return of the
child under the provisions of Article 12 may be refused if this would not be
permitted by the fundamental principles of the requested State relating to the
protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms.

Ms. R.P. does not rely
on any of the circumstances outlined in Article 13, nor on            Article
20.

[
13
.]                Articles 16
and 19 make it clear that no decision on the merits of the rights of     custody
form part of the court’s consideration until the court concludes that a child       should
not be returned; and that a decision not to return a child is not a determination
of         the merits of a custody dispute.

[
14
.]                Article 8
provides that any application under the
Convention
shall contain:

(a)        information
concerning the identity of the applicant, of                               the
child and of the person alleged to have removed or                               retained
the child;

(b)       where
available, the date of birth of the child;

(c)        the
grounds on which the applicant’s claim for return of                             the
child is based;

(d)       all
available information relating to the whereabouts of                               the
child and the indemnity of the person with whom the                 child is
presumed to be.

The application may be
accompanied or supplemented by –

(e)        an
authenticated copy of any relevant decision or                            agreement;

(f)        a
certificate or an affidavit emanating from a Central                                  Authority,
or other competent authority of State of the                                child’s
habitual residence, or from a qualified person,                                 concerning
the relevant law of that State;

(g)        any
other relevant document.

There
was no argument that this application was not procedurally compliant with            Article
8.

[
15
.]               Article
30 provides that:

Article 30

Any application
submitted to the Central Authorities or directly to the judicial or
administrative authorities of a Contracting State in accordance with the terms
of this Convention, together with documents and any other information appended
thereto or provided by a Central Authority, shall be admissible in the courts
or administrative authorities of the Contracting States.

The impact of Article
30 is to make admissible in this application an affidavit that would           otherwise
not form part of the evidence before this court: Mr. I.R.’s affidavit sworn on             April
22, 2016 in support of his Motion under the
Family Services Act
.

V.
THE
ISRAELI ORDER
:

[
16
.]                Included in
the material filed by the applicant are copies of documents in Hebrew          with
translations into English of what are called “Minutes” from the Court for
Family             Affairs in Rishon Lezion dated September 17, 2015 and signed
by Rivka Makais, Deputy   President.  They approve and validate a “Marital
Harmony and Alternatively Divorce             Agreement” (the “Agreement”)
signed by the parties on September 3, 2015. The latter          document
provides as follows at paragraphs 2.1, 3 and 4:

2.1      The parties
shall make an attempt to again live in the marital            harmony and to
conduct a good family life based on equality,       mutual understanding and
friendship.  The parties are signing on           this agreement based on a
genuine and honest hope that they will      never be forced to realize its
stipulations regarding separation       and divorce.

*          *          *

3.
Divorce
and Separation

In the
event that the parties attempt shall not be successful and        one of the
parties shall wish to separate, the party wishing to     separate shall notify
the other party.  Transfer of written notice                  whether by
personal delivery or by registered post shall be           evidence to receipt
of the separation notice.  Immediately on            delivery of the notice as
aforementioned the relationship between   the parties shall terminate and the
terms of this agreement         hereinafter shall be imposed.

4.
Divorce

4.1      The parties
shall file a joint petition for divorce at the Rabbinical     Court and each of
the parties undertakes to appear before the   Rabbinical court on the date and
time that the Court shall         determine, to sign on any document and to
take any action which  shall be required by the Honourable Rabbinical Court in
order to     enable the arrangement of the Jewish divorce (“Get”).

4.2      The husband
shall express his consent to provide the Jewish            divorce whereas the
wife shall express her consent to accept the      Jewish divorce and they shall
receive it.

4.3      Payments to
the Rabbinical Court in his matter          shall be paid by           the
couple in equal parts.

Paragraph 5 of the
Agreement provides for “Custody and visitation rights” in the           following
terms:

5.
Custody
and visitation rights

5.1.      The
minors shall remain in the joint guardianship of both their                                 parents.
The minors shall be in the custody of their mother and                              this
until they reach the age of 18 years.  Both parties recognize                                    the
minors’ need for both their      parents.

5.2.      The
parties undertake to care for and ensure all the needs and                                 requirements
of the minors to the best of their attention, to                          educate
them and supervise them with         devotion and loyalty                           with
constant and close cooperation in all matters relating to the                                minors.

5.3.      Any
decision regarding the education and/or medical and/or                                    emotional
treatment of the minor shall be taken        by both of                               parents
jointly.

5.4.        The
father and the mother undertake to transfer one to         the                               other
any information relating to the minors and each of them                                          undertakes
to be in contact with the educational and care                                        facilities.

[
17
.]                Paragraph 6 of
the agreement sets out the specific visitation and overnight           arrangements
for Mr. I.R..    It gives him visitation every Tuesday overnight, “every       second
alternate weekend” from school (at an unspecified day and time) until Sunday       morning
“at the start of the school day”.  Jewish festivals are distributed between          the
parties in paragraph 6.3.  Mr. I.R.’s time during the “long summer
vacation” is set           out in paragraph 6.5.

[
18
.]                Mr. I.R.’s
child support obligations are set in paragraph 7.  Paragraphs 8 to 12     provide
for the division of the parties’ property.

[
19
.]                The Agreement
specifically contemplates the family’s travel to Canada:

2.2.
The
parties wish that the entire family travel to Canada
for            a
lengthy period and/or

for the purpose of immigration     and settling
there
.  For this purpose the parties agree that            the wife shall
travel to Canada alone, prior to the husband          and the children and this
in order to investigate, clarify and            prepare for the move.

(emphasis
added)

[
20
.]                From Mr. I.R’s
perspective, the critical portion of the Agreement is found at       paragraph
2.3, which provides that:

2.3.     If and
inasmuch as the parties and the family shall move to  Canada, the parties agree
that each of the couple shall be            permitted, at any stage, to advise
the other that he/she wishes to   return to Israel and the remaining spouse
shall be obligated to            cooperate and to take action in order to bring
about the return of     the family to Israel as quickly as possible while
causing    minimum damage to the parties’ children and the parties’           property.

[
21
.]                The Minutes
engraft onto those provisions the following:

In the matter of that
stated in Sections 2.2 and 2.3 we have return tickets in
June 2016
and
we
are returning because we have an active business which we operate during the
summer.

It is agreed that
contrary
to that stated in the agreement
,
the decision as to whether the entire
family will remain in Canada or return to live in Israel will be made jointly

by both parents and pursuant to that stated in the agreement by the planned
date of return in June 2016.

Pursuant to that
agreed,
it is sufficient that if one of the parents will wish to return to
live in Israel, the entire family shall return to live in Israel.

(all emphasis added)

VI.
ISRAELI
LEGISLATION
:

[
22
.]                Page 199 of
the Record on Application is an “authorized translation” of the State           of
Israel’s
Capacity and Guardianship Law
, 5722-1962.  It reads as follows
in its     entirety:

CHAPTER TWO: PARENTS
AND MINOR CHILDREN

Status of parents

14.      Parents shall
be the natural guardians of their minor children.

Functions of parents.

15.      The
guardianship of the parents shall include the duty and the                     right
to take care of the needs of the minor, including his             education,
studies, vocational and occupation training and work,           and to
preserve, manage and develop his property; it shall also       include the
right to the custody of the minor, to determine his  place of residence and the
authority to act on his behalf.

[
23
.]               There is
nothing in the material submitted that addresses the question of whether            the
Minutes supersede this legislation.

VII.
THE
FACTUAL BACKGROUND
:

A.        The
Family’s Circumstances:

[
24
.]                The parties and the
children are all Israeli citizens.  Mr. I.R. and Ms. R.P. married on June 8,
2004 in Israel.

[
25
.]                According to
the Request for Return of Abducted Children (“the Request”) signed        by
Yuval Kaplinsky on June 30, 2016, I.R. is 36 years of age (date of birth […],
1980); he is a chef;  R.P. is presently 37 years of age (date of birth   […],
1979); she is also a chef.

[
26
.]                The three R.'s
children were all born in Israel, A.R. on […], 2007  (making him 9 years of
age) and twins L.R. and D.R. on […], 2010 (making them    6 years of age).

[
27
.]                Until moving
to New Brunswick in October 2015 the children lived in Israel with           their
parents.

[
28
.]                According to
paragraph 8.1 of the Agreement, “during their marriage, the parties            built
a residence on farm land belonging to the husband’s family”.

[
29
.]                At an
undisclosed date in 2011 the parties began taking the steps necessary to     immigrate
to Canada.    Mr. I.R. described the efforts at paragraph 6 of his affidavit    sworn
on April 22, 2016 in support of his
Family Services Act
Motion:

6.        While the
respondent and I were still married in 2011 we     applied to immigrate to
Canada as a family.  After a long   and expensive process and the breakdown of
our marriage          we were advised our application had been successful.

[
30
.]                At paragraph
19 of her affidavit sworn on September 19, 2016 Ms. R.P.  deposed that:

19.      The move to
Fredericton was the end of a long process of    applying to immigrate to Canada
and including seeking out a      sponsor, meeting with sponsor during a
previous trip to Canada,       engaging in negotiations to join in business
ventures in Saint         John and Fredericton, and ultimately agree [sic] to
purchase the            C[…] Café, a restaurant in Fredericton.

[
31
.]                In paragraph
13 of her affidavit, Ms. R.P. deposed that:

13.      At the time
we moved, it was discussed and intended that we           would move to Canada,
traveling to Israel and attend [sic] to the         profitable business
there while we grew out [sic] business        venture            Canada.

[
32
.]                The material
filed discloses that both parties held US visas, Mr. I.R. for a ten      year
period from June 22, 2004 and Ms. R.P. for a ten year period from July            2000.
There was no reference in either counsel’s submissions or the material filed
with

respect to the visas or
the reason why the parties held them.

[
33
.]                The
Confirmation of Nomination to a Provincial Nominee (New Brunswick         Provincial
Nominee Program) confirmed the family’s nomination date of March 3, 2014          and
the consideration by Citizen and Immigration Canada of the family’s application
for            permanent residents’ visas.

[
34
.]                Ms. R.P.
arrived in New Brunswick on October 4, 2015.  Mr. I.R.            followed with
the children on October 16, 2015.  All of the family members became   permanent
residents of Canada, Ms. R.P. on October 4, 2015 and Mr. I.R.      and the
children on October 16, 2015, the dates of their respective entries into New             Brunswick.

[
35
.]                According to
the material filed, every family member submitted to various          medical
examinations required for their visa applications.  The “eMedical Information      Sheets”
for each member of the family appear at pages 60 to 64 of the Record on    Application.

[
36
.]                The family
lived in Fredericton in a rented home located at T[…] Court.              An
inquiry made by Mr. I.R. (apparently sometime in January 2016) with respect to     purchasing
the property was met with a response that the price was “$295,000.00 with all       furniture
and appliances. $280,000.00 without”.  (See Exhibit C to Ms. R.P.’s  affidavit
sworn on September 19, 2016).  The purchase apparently did not take place.  No         other
evidence was offered with respect to the potential or plans for any purchase.

[
37
.]                The parties
and the children lived together in the T[…] Court property until         April
5, 2016 when Mr. I.R. left the relationship and the home.  Ms. R.P. and  the
children have continued to live in that home.

[
38
.]                The children
were enrolled in schools in Fredericton after their arrival in New      Brunswick
and they have returned to their respective schools. A.R. attends L[…] Middle
School and the twins attend F[…] Elementary School.

[
39
.]                According to the
affidavit of Ms. R.P., she and Mr. I.R. worked at the C[…] Café in Fredericton as
part of a business arrangement to purchase the restaurant from its owners. (See
paragraph 101 of her affidavit).  In addition, the parties operated a stall at
the C[…] Market in Fredericton on Saturdays selling “various food items and we
regularly earned $700.00 or more in profit after the costs”.  (See paragraphs
98 and 99 of her affidavit).

[
40
.]                Ms. R.P.
deposed that she has brought a claim “against the vendors of the           C[…]
Café” “in an attempt to recover equipment and pay for work”.  (See paragraph  102
of her affidavit).

[
41
.]                Mr. I.R. wrote as
follows to an unidentified (in the translation) friend and on an unidentified
(in the translation) date that:

It’s better than I
thought it will be.  I don’t see myself coming back to live in Israel, maybe
just to come back to work at the macabi
in the summer.  The prices of
the vegetables and the fruits like gold.  I think you will be set in here.  The
ground is for free and you do not pay for water.

(emphasis added)

[
42
.]

The
material filed is contradictory with respect to the parties’ marital status.        According
to Ms. R.P.’s affidavit, at paragraph 10:

My
understanding is that under the law of Israel, while we were granted divorce by
the Rabbinical Court, our civil status remains as a married couple as we have
chosen to resume cohabitation.  In Israel, the civil family court has no
jurisdiction to adjudicate the divorce status.

[
43
.]                At paragraph 4
of his affidavit filed in support of his
Family Services Act
Motion,          Mr.
I.R. deposed that he and Ms. R.P. “were divorced in September 2015 by        an
official Divorce Order and Separation Agreement in Israel”.

[
44
.]                The relevance
of the parties’ marital status is perhaps remote.  The Minutes and   the
Agreement that they incorporate clearly contemplated the parties’ continued
shared          residence and their move to Canada, notwithstanding their
divorce in the Rabbinical       Court and any subsequent separation.

[
45
.]                The material filed
with, and in response to, the application is somewhat conflicting with respect
to when there were discussions regarding returning to Israel. In the affidavit
filed by Mr. I.R. in support of his
Family Services Act
Motion, he
deposed to a conversation in February 2016 during which the parties “had a
disagreement about whether we should return to Israel as a family unit or if we
should remain in Canada”.  Mr. I.R. goes on to depose to being advised sometime
in March 2016 by Ms. R.P. that the children’s passports had been placed for
safekeeping by her with a friend.  In paragraph 12 of his affidavit, Mr. I.R.
deposes that he went to work on April 5, 2016 and returned home to find that his
personal belongings had been left outside of their residence.  According to
him, Ms. R.P. told him that he was no longer welcome in the home and she
threatened to call the police and make allegations of abuse against him.

[
46
.]                In the affidavit
filed by Ms. R.P. in response to this application, she deposes to demands that
she says were made by Mr. I.R. in late March 2016 for daily sex; his threats
that he would leave and take the children with him

if
she refused him daily sex; her call to a friend asking the friend to come and
take the passports so that Mr. I.R. could not take the children away; her
telephone call to her mother, who told Ms. R.P. to stay strong because she was
coming to Fredericton in June; a disagreement with Mr. I.R. at the C[…] Café on
April 5th, 2016 during which she informed him that she wanted to separate; and
the ensuing threat made by  Mr. I.R. that if she left him he would take the
children back to Israel without her.  She also deposes to Mr. I.R.’s refusal to
let her have the keys to the family vehicle; his withdrawal of all of the money
in the parties’ joint bank account which left her with no financial resources;
and his subsequent advice to her that he would no longer provide her with any
financial support.

[
47
.]                As was noted by
counsel for the Attorney-General, much of the contents of Ms. R.P.’s affidavit
speaks to events that are not relevant to this application given that this is
not a hearing designed to address the best interests of the children. Counsel
for Ms. R.P. confirmed on the record that Ms. R.P. was not relying on the
“grave risk of harm” exception contained in Article 13 of the
Convention
despite
the allegations in her affidavit that Mr. I.R. has been sexually inappropriate
with L.R..

[
48
.]                In the absence of
an opportunity to hear and observe the parties, it is not possible to form any
impressions of credibility.  What appears to be incontrovertible is that they
separated on April 5, 2016.  When exactly Mr. I.R. made the demand to return to
Israel is not so incontrovertible, however, he filed his Preliminary Notice of
Motion under the
Family Services Act
on April 22, 2016 in which he asked
for a custody order “for the purpose of returning to Israel with the children”.
Mr. I.R.’s clarion call has consistently been paragraph 2.3 of the Agreement,
as set out above at paragraph 20.   (I note parenthetically that he does not
appear to view the financial obligations imposed on him by that same Agreement
as binding as what he asserts is the right given to him by paragraph 2.3).

[
49
.]                The date on which
the wrongful retention is alleged to have taken place is identified in the
second Request at the last paragraph of “Part IV.  Time, date, place and
circumstances of the removal or retention”:

The mother travelled
to Canada on 4 October 2015.  The father and the children joined her on 14
October 2015. As noted above, the parents’ agreement was that the entire family
would return to Israel regardless of any future decisions on 21 June 2016, however,
the mother did not allow the children to return to Israel with the father and
hid the children’s passports from the father. (See page 13 of the Record on
Application).

This information appears to
ignore the references in the Minutes/Agreement that confirm that the planned
return in June was for the purpose of attending to the parties’ seasonal
business.  Nor is it specific as to the date on which Ms. R.P. “hid the
children’s passports”.

[
50
.]                As noted above, the
first Requisition was filed on May 17, 2016.  At page 130 of the Record on
Application, and under paragraph 5. “Time, Place, Date and Circumstances of
Wrongful Removal or Retention”, the Request states that since April 5, 2015,  “I.R.
was been denied custody of and access to the children” and “the children have
therefore been wrongfully retained against the express direction of the prior
Agreement between I.R. and R.P.”.

[
51
.]                There was no
explanation offered for the difference in the dates of the alleged wrongful
retention.

[
52
.]                Both
Requisitions give Mr. I.R.’s current residence as “the City of Fredericton    (no
fixed address) in the County of Queen’s [sic]”.  He is not living in Israel.
The       Request indicates that the habitual residence of all of the family
members is “[…],         Petahya, Israel”.   Why that would be shown as Ms.
R.P.’s habitual residence,             given the parties’ divorce and their
subsequent separation, was not explained.

[
53
.]                Ms. R.P., at
paragraphs 93 to 97 of her affidavit, deposed that:

93.      Our joint
bank account in Israel is the main account for our                        company’s
deposits earned from a catering business, rental of         equipment and
rental income.

94.      The annual
turnover of funds in this account is more than    $250,000 with approximately
$100,000 in profit.

95.
It was for
this reason we were to go to Israel in June, to   attend to business during the
festival season.

96.      The applicant
told me that the only reason he wants to take the        children to Israel is
that I do not want to go, and that asking the             Court to make them go

VIII.
LAW
AND ANALYSIS
:

[
63
.]

The
jurisprudence has made it clear that an application pursuant to the
Convention

is not a determination of the best interests of the child who is the subject of
the application.
See:
Thomson v. Thomson
1994 CanLII 26 (SCC)
,
1994 Carswell Man 91
S.C.C.;

Pollastro v. Pollastro
1999 CanLII 3702 (ON CA)
,
1999 Carswell Ont 848 (C.A.)
;
Gallardo Bazan
v. MacDonald
2011 Carswell Ont 13392 (S.C.J.)
;
New Brunswick (Attorney
General) v. M.(A.P.)

2010 CarswellNB 550 (Q.B.)
.

[
64
.]                 “
The starting point in
a return application is to determine if a child has,                  in fact,
been wrongfully removed or retained under the
Hague            Convention
.
In order to be wrongfully removed or retained
the child      must have been
removed from his or her habitual residence or    retained in a country other
than his or her habitual residence
”

Fasiang
v. Fasiangova

2008 BCSC 1339 (CanLII)
,
2008 Carswell BC 2096 (S.C.)
at paragraph
11
.

(emphasis
added)

[
65
.]                A
person applying for an order for the return of a child under the
Convention
bears
the onus of establishing on a balance of probabilities that:

•

the
requesting state is the child’s habitual residence;

•

according
to the law of the state of habitual residence,       he/she had a right of
custody; and that he/she was            exercising at the time of the
removal/retention; and

•

the
removal/retention was wrongful and done without        his/her consent or
acquiescence.

See:
J.T., Jr. v. S.L.T.
2016
CarswellOnt 2116 (S.C.J.)
, at paragraph 8
;
deHaan v. Gracia

2004
CarswellAlta 224 (Q.B.)
at paragraph 38
.

[
66
.]                There is no
definition of “habitual residence” in the
Convention
.  As the British
Columbia Court of Appeal held in
Chan v. Chow
2001 Carswell BC 868
, at
paragraph 51
, quoting from
Re J (a minor) (Abduction: Custody Rights)
,

[1990] 2 A.C. 562 (U.K.H.L)
, the term “habitual residence”:

is to be understood
according to the ordinary and natural meaning of the two words.  It is a
question of fact to be decided by reference to all the circumstances.
It is
established by residing in a place for an appreciable period of time with a
“settled intention”.
A child’s habitual residence is tied to the habitual
residence of his or her custodian.

(emphasis
added)

See
also:
Korutowska-Wooff v. Wooff
2003 CarswellOnt 6181 (S.C.J.)
;
Ellis
v. Wentzell-            Ellis

2010 ONCA 347 (CanLII)
,
2010 CarswellOnt 2981 (C.A.)
.

[
67
.]               The Ontario Superior
Court of Justice recently considered the issue of “habitual residence”.  In
J.T.,
Jr. v. S.L.T,
above, at paragraph 11, the court held that:

•

The
question of habitual residence is a question of fact to be           determined
based on the circumstances.

•

A
habitual residence is the place where a person resides for "an       appreciable
period of time" with "a settled intention" to do so.

•

In
order to be recognized as a habitual residence, the residence        must be
adopted voluntarily.

•

The
existence of a "settled intention" is determined by reference      to
intention immediately prior to the physical move to the new   residence.

•

A
young child's habitual residence is determined by the habitual      residence
of his custodial parent(s). If only one parent has legal   custody of a child,
that child's habitual residence is the place            where that parent had a
settled intention to reside and in which   he or she did reside for an
appreciable period.

•

If
a child's parents have joint custody, then that child's habitual       residence
is the place where his parents jointly had a settled        intention to reside
and where they did reside for an appreciable  period. The intention must be
joint; one parent cannot            unilaterally change a child's habitual
residence.

•

Parties
need not intend a place to be their permanent home for it      to be deemed
their habitual residence under the Convention. All    that is required is their
residence in that place for an appreciable  period of time.

•

Settled
intention alone is not sufficient to establish a habitual           residence.
The child actually has to move and be there for an   appreciable time.

[
68
.]                In
Wirta v. Wirta

2016 CarswellOnt 9337 (S.C.J.)
, MacKinnon, J. held at paragraphs 41 to 43
as follows:

41.      In this case, since the parties shared legal
decision-making   custodial rights for their children, the court must determine
the   shared intentions of the parents with respect to the relocation to      Ontario.

The question is: immediately before the physical  move, were the parties
jointly intending to move to Ottawa        with the children and to stay there,
temporarily or    permanently, for a particular purpose
, which could be            employment
or family? If so,             does the evidence establish that          the
children have in fact settled   into the new location to the     extent that
they have acquired a new habitual residence? (
See        Csoke v. Fustos,
2013 ONSC 2417
(CanLII)
, at para.

260
).

42.      Where the parties’ evidence on their
intentions is contradictory,       the court is instructed not to take their
representations at face     value, but rather
to determine based on all the
evidence,    including their actions, whether the parents had already            agreed
to change the children’s habitual residence
(
Ellis
, at           para.
17
).

43.
The
actions of the parties prior to the physical move clearly         reveal a
joint endeavour to relocate, with the children, to            Ottawa, on an
indefinite basis,
for the purpose of Ms. Wirta’s     employment. The
parties discussed Ms. Wirta’s possible            employment transfer and,
after discussing it, Ms. Wirta applied        for the transfer. When she was
successful in obtaining the   transfer, the parties jointly leased a house in
Ottawa. They           undertook the process of immigrating to Canada: Ms.
Wirta            filled out the paperwork and Mr. Wirta signed various          documents
and underwent a medical examination. They shipped      their household
furnishings and belongings from Washington  State to Ottawa. I conclude that
the parties carried out a joint    plan to relocate to Ottawa with the
children.

(all
emphasis added)

The court in
Wirta
dismissed
the return application, holding that the children’s habitual residence was
Canada.

[
69
.]                A “settled intention”
or purpose is an intent to stay in a place, whether temporarily or permanently,
for a particular purpose or several purposes.  See:
H.(A.) v. H.
(F.S.)

2013 CarswellOnt 2510 (S.C.J.)
;
Chan v. Chow
, above;
Schroeder v.
McCormack

2016 CarswellOnt 10370 (S.C.J.)
.

[
70
.]                In the latter case,
McDermot, J. held at paragraph 53 that:

53.      The intent of
the parties
need not be to reside permanently             in the
jurisdiction in question; a temporary move to that            jurisdiction will
do
:
see
Wentzell-Ellis
and H.(A.)

v.    H.(F.S.)
,
2013 ONSC
1308 (CanLII)
at para.
52
as aff’d by
Hammerschmidt v. Hammerschmidt
,

2013 ONCA 227          (CanLII)
.  Krusack J. in
H.(A.)
also noted that
“intention
is            examined through one’s actions”
and that is what I have to         look
to in this case in order to determine habitual residency.             In the
words of Ms. Ng, I have to look at the
“facts on the   ground” to determine
who intended what.

(emphasis
added)

See also:
Unger v.
Unger

2016 CarswellOnt 10374 (S.C.J.)
at paragraph 23
.

[
71
.]                Justice Donna
Martinson, in her
decision in
Fasiang v. Fasiangova
,
above, at
paragraphs
60 to 64
discussed the concept of  “settled intention” by reference
to several decisions and authorities:

60.
A settled intention or purpose requires that “the purpose of living where one
does has a sufficient degree of continuity to be properly described as
settled.” But all that is required is that there is a settled purpose. There is
no requirement that there be an intention to settle indefinitely:
R. v.
Barnet London Borough Council

(1982),
[1983] 2 A.C. 309 (U.K. H.L.)
at 344,

cited in
Chan
at para. 33.

61
Further, a settled intention or purpose describes one’s purpose for living
where one does and it can be for a limited period. If there is a settled
intention or purpose “it will stand out clearly as a matter of general
impression”: Chesire and North’s Private International Law, 13th ed. (London:
Butterworths, 1999) at 166-167, cited in Chan at para. 34.

62
A settled intention or purpose is “an intent to stay in a place whether
temporarily or permanently for a particular purpose, such as employment,
family, etc.”:
Korutowska-Wooff v. Wooff

(2004),
2004 CanLII 5548 (ON CA)
,
242 D.L.R. (4th) 385
(Ont. C.A.)
at para.
8
, (2004), 188 O.A.C. 376 (Ont. C.A.).

63
Madam Justice Stromberg-Stein listed the following factors that may be
considered in determining settled intention at para. 36
in
Petnehazi v.
Kresz
,
1999 CanLII 6078 (BC SC)
,
[1999] B.C.J. No. 1238 (B.C. S.C.)
, this list is not exhaustive:

1.
Both parties have relocated to the new                                              state;

2.
The custodial parent is employed in the                                            new
state;

3.
The custodial parent had taken steps to                                             satisfy
the immigration requirements of                                            the
new state;

4.
The children were enrolled in school in                                            the
new            state;

5.
The parents had purchased one-way                                     tickets
to the new state; and

6.
Accommodation has been arranged in                                              the
new state.

64
Settled intent to change habitual residence is determined just prior to the
physical move to the new habitual residence:
deHaan v. Gracia

(2004),

351 A.R. 354 (Alta. Q.B.)
at para.
32
,
2004 ABQB 74 (Alta. Q.B.)
.

[
72
.]                The Ontario
Court of Appeal recently
held in
Balev v. Baggott

2016 ONCA        680

at paragraph
42
that:

42.      The Ontario
courts have uniformly held that a parent’s consent        to a
time-limited
stay
does not shift the child’s habitual          residence:
see
Ellis
v. Wentzell-Ellis
; Unger v. Unger
,
2016            ONSC 4258 (CanLII)
, 2016
ONSC 4258 (S.C.), at para.
57
;
Webb v. Gaudaur
,
2015 ONSC 6956

(S.C.)
;
Fulmer v. Kaleo-          Fulmer
,
[2002] O.J. No. 3183 (S.C.)
,
at para. 18
;
Solem v.     Solem
,
2013 ONSC 1097 (CanLII)
, 2013 ONSC 1097
(S.C.), at    paras.
37-38
; and
Snetzko v. Snetzko

(1996),
65 A.C.W.S.
(3d)     56
(Ont. Ct. (Gen. Div.)), at para. 25.

(emphasis
added)

This
conclusion seems at odds with the court’s comments in paragraph 61 of
Fasiang
v. Fasiangova
, above.  However, the Ontario Court of Appeal did not
“foreclose the possibility that there may be cases where a consensual time-limited
stay is so long that it becomes time-limited in name only and the child’s
habitual residence has changed”.  (See paragraph 49).  Nor did the Ontario
Court of Appeal distinguish or reverse its
decision in
Korutowska-Wooff v.
Wooff
,
above,

that the intention to stay in a place “whether
temporarily or permanently for a particular purpose” could be sufficient.

[
73
.]
In
Fasiang
,
Martinson, J. also undertook an analysis of some of the jurisprudence           with
respect to the principle that the new residence must have been “for an
appreciable           period of time”:

69       Whether
residence has been for an appreciable period of time is      a question of
fact:
Nessa v. Chief Adjudication Officer
,
[1999] 1   W.L.R. 1937
at 1942 (H.L.)
.

70         An
appreciable period of time is not a fixed period:
Nessa
at         1943.

71        An
appreciable period of time could be as short as one        day:
Garbolino
at
para. 4.6,
cited in
deHaan
at para.
42
.

72       Nine
months has been held to be easily long enough:
Chan
at
para. 44. One month has also been held to be long enough:
F.
(A   Minor) (Child Abduction), Re
(1991), [1992] 1 F.L.R. 548
(Eng.            C.A.) at
555. The Ontario Superior Court of Justice found that a    mother acquired
habitual residence in her new location upon            arrival, and the
children since they acquired their mother's   habitual residence also acquired
a new habitual residence upon             arrival:
Braatelien v.
Horning
,
[2001] O.J. No. 3799
(Ont.    S.C.J.)
at para.
4
.

73        Factors
to take into account when determining whether        residence has been for an
appreciable period of time such that   habitual residence has been established
can include, but are not     limited to: bringing personal possession to the
new country;            taking the necessary steps to establish residence
before travelling     to the new country; having a right of abode in the new
country;            seeking to bring family members to the new country; and,
having     "durable ties" with the new country:
Nessa
at
1942.

74       The
threshold for what constitutes an appreciable period of time      will be
different if the party is resuming habitual residence in a       location
rather than establishing residence in the location for the             first
time:
Nessa
at 1943.

[
74
.]                Using the
principles articulated in these various decisions, this court’s analysis     and
conclusions are as follows.

[
75
.]                Mr. I.R. and Ms.
R.P. began the immigration process in 2011 and             pursued it for four
years.  All of the family members became permanent residents of  Canada.  The
evidence does not support a conclusion that the stay was “time limited”,   rather,
that it was indefinite, a relocation for the purpose of living and working in
New             Brunswick.  The parties’ intention to return to Israel in June
of 2016 was so they could   run their seasonal business.  This intention is
clearly documented in the          Minutes/Agreement that both parties signed,
in Ms. R.P.’s affidavit, and in         Exhibit B to Ms. R.P.’s affidavit.  The
parties followed through with their             relocation/immigration plans
even in the face of their divorce.  I conclude that the parties           had a
demonstrated intention to settle in New Brunswick and that it was in place when
they and their children moved to his province in October 2015.

[
76
.]                The
Minutes/Agreement gave the parties “joint guardianship” of the children.      However,
in the event of a separation they also gave Ms. R.P. the custody of the    children
until they reached 18 years of age.  Mr. I.R. was given visitation rights.  The
Agreement is specific with respect to the joint decision making in
the areas of “education    and/or medical and/or emotional treatment of the
minors”.  It is entirely silent with             respect to the authority to
decide the children’s residence.  However, the parties jointly  had a settled
intention to move to and reside in New Brunswick.  The family lived here           from
early October 2015.  Mr. I.R.’s decision to return to Israel was made
unilaterally      and after he and Ms. R.P. had physically separated.  Mr. I.R.
relies upon the     provision in the Minutes/Agreement that appears to give one
parent the right to   unilaterally change the family’s residence and effect the
return of the family to Israel.           Although paragraph 2.3 of the
Minutes/Agreement may be interpreted to give one parent  the right to effect
the return of the family, that provision is not dispositive of the          determination
of the children’s habitual residence and certainly not for the period prior to         the
exercise by Mr. I.R. of any such unilateral decision making right.

[
77
.]                The adoption
by the parties of their residence in New Brunswick was entirely      voluntary
and the decision was a joint one.  The parties had maintained an intention to         move
to New Brunswick for a period in excess of four years.  Even in the face of
their         divorce, Mr. I.R. followed Ms. R.P. to New Brunswick bringing the
children     with him, as had been the plan.  The parties began running their
restaurant business, as    had been the plan.

[
78
.]                The children
moved to New Brunswick with their parents and were immediately            enrolled
in school. They lived in a home with their parents.  They had permanent       resident
status.  They resided together as a family in New Brunswick from October       2015
until the parties separated in April 2016.  Given all of the facts, it is the
view of this       court that this period of residence was for an appreciable
time.

[
79
.]                There was at least
one inquiry made with respect to the parties’ purchase of their rented             home.
They acquired a vehicle here.  Mr. I.R. wrote to a friend saying that he did
not see himself going back to live in Israel.

[
80
.]                The parties worked
in New Brunswick in their chosen professional fields pursuant to an arrangement
with the owner of a local café that Ms. R.P. described as “a business
arrangement to purchase the restaurant from the owners”.  (See paragraph 101 of
her affidavit).  They also worked part of every weekend selling food at a local
cultural market.  There was nothing in the material filed to suggest that these
ventures were not financially viable.  Although the parties apparently
maintained a bank account in Israel, the account was connected to the operation
of the seasonal business in that country.  The parties established at least one
joint bank account in New Brunswick.

[
81
.]                The fact that
the parties purchased return tickets is not conclusive of the  characterization
of their stay as one that was time-limited.  It is clear from a consideration         of
all of the evidence, including the parties’ actions, that the move to New
Brunswick    was for an indefinite period.  The reason behind the purchase of
return tickets is equally         clear: the parties intended to travel back to
Israel and manage their seasonal business.

[
82
.]                It is the
conclusion of this court that the facts establish that the habitual residence           of
all three R.'s children as of April 5, 2016, and/or April 20, 2016, and/or June
21,    2016 was the Province of New Brunswick, Canada, and not the State of
Israel.  The      application is therefore dismissed.  There will be no order
for the return of the children.

Their passports
shall be released immediately to R.P..
